title: Composting at Home - A Beginner's Guide for 2026
excerpt: Learn how to start composting at home, what you can and cannot compost, and how it helps the environment in 2026.
content:
What Is Home Composting?

Composting is the natural process of recycling organic waste, such as food scraps and yard trimmings, into a rich soil amendment called compost. Microorganisms break down the material over time, creating a dark, crumbly substance that improves soil structure, retains moisture, and supplies nutrients to plants.

What Can I Compost at Home?

You can compost fruit and vegetable scraps, coffee grounds, tea bags, eggshells, yard trimmings, leaves, grass clippings, and plain paper or cardboard. Avoid meat, fish, dairy, greasy foods, pet waste, diseased plants, and weeds that have gone to seed, as these can attract pests, create odors, or spread plant diseases.

How Do I Start Composting in My Backyard?

Choose a dry, shady spot near a water source. Set up a compost bin or pile, then layer brown materials (dry leaves, straw, cardboard) with green materials (food scraps, fresh grass clippings). Aim for roughly three parts brown to one part green by volume. Keep the pile damp like a wrung-out sponge and turn it every week or two to add air. In two to six months, depending on conditions, you will have finished compost.

Can I Compost If I Live in an Apartment?

Yes. Indoor options include worm bins (vermicomposting), bokashi fermentation, and countertop electric composters. Worm bins are odor-free when maintained properly and fit under a kitchen sink. Bokashi systems ferment food waste in a sealed bucket. Electric composters dehydrate and grind scraps quickly but are not true compost and should be mixed with soil before use.

How Does Composting Help the Environment?

Composting keeps organic waste out of landfills, where it decomposes without oxygen and produces methane, a potent greenhouse gas. According to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, food is the single largest category of material sent to municipal landfills. Composting also reduces the need for chemical fertilizers, improves soil health, and helps sequester carbon in the ground.

How Do I Know When Compost Is Ready?

Finished compost is dark brown, crumbly, and smells earthy like soil. You should no longer recognize the original food scraps or yard waste. It should not be hot in the center, indicating the decomposition process is complete. If the material is still lumpy or smells sour, it needs more time.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does composting take?

A well-maintained backyard pile produces compost in two to six months. Cold composting with minimal turning can take six to twelve months. Indoor worm bins typically yield usable compost in two to three months. Electric countertop units process scraps in hours, though the output needs curing before it is true compost.

Does composting smell bad?

A properly managed compost pile should smell earthy, not rotten. Bad odors usually mean the pile is too wet, lacks air, or contains forbidden materials such as meat or dairy. Turning the pile, adding dry brown materials, and removing problem items fixes most odor issues.

Can I compost paper and cardboard?

Yes, but avoid glossy paper, coated cardboard, and paper with heavy ink or plastic liners. Plain newspaper, uncoated cardboard, paper bags, and paper towels (without chemical cleaners) are good brown materials. Tear them into small pieces to speed decomposition.

Do I need a special bin to compost?

No. You can compost in a simple pile on the ground, though a bin keeps it neater and deters animals. You can build a bin from wood pallets, wire mesh, or a plastic storage container with holes drilled for air flow.

What do I do with finished compost?

Mix compost into garden soil before planting, spread it as a top dressing around existing plants, or blend it into potting mix for containers. It improves drainage in clay soil and water retention in sandy soil. You can also make compost tea by steeping finished compost in water and using the liquid to water plants.

Is composting legal in my city?

Most U.S. cities allow backyard composting, but some homeowners associations and municipalities have rules about bin placement, pile size, or acceptable materials. Check your local ordinances or HOA rules before starting, especially in urban areas where rodent concerns may apply.

Sources: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Composting at Home (as of November 2026); U.S. Department of Agriculture, Natural Resources Conservation Service, Soil Health guidance (as of November 2026); Cornell Waste Management Institute, Composting Resources (as of November 2026); Institute for Local Self-Reliance, Community Composting (as of November 2026).
